scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Tracing its roots to 15th-century southern Mozambique, the dance's name translates from Xitsonga as "hitting to the rhythm."
This is Xibelani. 15th century or earlier.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (wENXN_g4mtM)
Title card: Xibelani · South Africa · 15th century or earlier

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The history of the xibelani dance reaches back to the early coastal societies of southern Mozambique from the 1400s or earlier, where tribes experimented with wooden instruments and percussion.
The Chopi people became central to this development through the timbila, now a UNESCO Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.
Over centuries, the tradition took deep root among the Tsonga women of Limpopo and Mpumalanga.

Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Tsonga girls learn xibelani to express pride in their cultural heritage.

It is performed during specific cultural practices such as mkhinyavezo and Ku chachula, accompanies dances like makhwaya and mchongolo, and features prominently at xiseveseve parties, church services, and rituals.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance style requires the performer to shake their hips in tune with the rhythm while using the entire body to guide the movement.
Dancers tie a voluminous skirt around the waist to visually amplify the rapid, high-speed shaking motion, which follows a complicated routine customary to the Tsonga people.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear a specialized skirt called a tinguvu.
Historically made from grass, strings, wool, and various fibers, modern tinguvu are long, strong cloth garments designed to create a visual swirl when the hips shake.
Performances occur outdoors during community gatherings, inside churches, at ritual events, and on stages alongside Tsonga bands.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The Chopi people are documented as the historical source for the foundational musical and percussion forms associated with the wider tradition.
The dance is practiced across the Limpopo and Mpumalanga provinces of South Africa, with historical ties extending into southern Mozambique.
Linked historically with the musical traditions of the Chopi people and modernly associated with Tsonga ndzhumbha and Tsonga disco.

music_brief.purpose: original soundtrack faithful to the tradition, with documented commercial reuse rights and no recurring royalties
music_brief.rights_rule: A composition brief does not clear an output. Record the provider/model/version, terms and date, input rights, output licence, restrictions and review before release.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Xibelani (South Africa). New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.

wardrobe.policy: neutral dress with a respectful nod (palette and fabric only): the sources describe sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire, or the dance is sacred
